Lessons.Title: To the Number Line
ExplanationParagraphs: In the original 2021 warm-up Notice and Wonder: Two Number Lines, students compare number-line representations and notice that lengths smaller than one whole can be represented as equal intervals. Discuss what stays the same about the distance from 0 to 1, rather than treating tick marks as isolated objects.

Activity 1 is a nine-card, open-ended classification task (A–I), NOT nine predetermined answers to one category: A 0–8 two intervals (step 4); B 0–1 four intervals (step 1/4); C 0–3 six intervals (step 1/2); D 0–2 four intervals (step 1/2); E 0–4 four intervals (step 1); F 0–1 six intervals (step 1/6); G 0–6 three intervals (step 2); H 0–2 six intervals (step 1/3); I 0–4 eight intervals (step 1/2). The original SVG assets for all nine cards were read from the owner-device 2021 teacher HTML. Possible categories overlap and include 0-to-1 unit fractional partition vs intervals greater than 1, same interval length despite different endpoints, or multi-whole number lines. Teacher assesses mathematical justification of the student's chosen groups.

Activity 2 contrasts two correct ways of using 1/2: Andre marks the LENGTH of each half-interval (each spans one half) while Clare labels the POINT halfway between zero and one. A mathematical number line locates numbers at ticks; distance statements describe the segments between ticks. Do not treat the two label placements as competing incorrect answers; ask pupils how both representations can make sense.

The original five hands-on fold-and-label tasks each use a fresh 0-to-1 line: fold into halves and locate 1/2; thirds and locate 1/3; fourths and locate 1/4; sixths and locate 1/6; eighths and locate 1/8. Make equally spaced marks and keep endpoints 0 and 1 fixed. Partners share their folding strategies; teachers check physical equal-length folding and explanations, not a fraction string alone.

Whole-number number lines with labels beyond 1 are not fraction strips whose right endpoint is always 1: cards A, C, D, E, G, H and I extend beyond 1. For example, card I runs from 0 to 4 with half-step intervals, whereas card F runs 0 to 1 with sixth-step intervals. Count spaces, not merely printed numbers or marks; the step size is (right endpoint − left endpoint)/number of equal intervals.

KeyConcepts.Title: Unit on the number line
KeyConcepts.Definition: The segment from 0 to 1 is one entire unit, whatever the printed width of the drawing.
KeyConcepts.Rule: 1/n of that unit is the length of one of n equal segments between 0 and 1.
KeyConcepts.Example: Four equal steps across 0 to 1 locate 1/4, 2/4, 3/4, 1.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fraction as a point
KeyConcepts.Definition: The fraction k/n denotes the number at the end of k successive 1/n intervals from zero.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Mark a point at k/n; distinguish the label of a point from the length of a segment.
KeyConcepts.Example: A tick midway between 0 and 1 is the number 1/2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Interval size from endpoints
KeyConcepts.Definition: The length of one equal interval is the total span divided by the count of intervals.
KeyConcepts.Rule: step=(right−left)/equal interval count; the same count of marks may represent very different lengths.
KeyConcepts.Example: 0–8 with 2 intervals means each interval is 4; 0–1 with 4 intervals means each is 1/4.

KeyConcepts.Title: More than one whole
KeyConcepts.Definition: A line from zero beyond one includes multiple complete unit lengths.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Use one unit 0 to 1 as reference when labeling fractional points beyond 1.
KeyConcepts.Example: Card I has half-step marks across four whole units, including 3/2 and 7/2.

WorkedExamples.Title: Card A — large-number intervals
WorkedExamples.Question: Card A shows 0, one middle tick, and 8. What is each step?
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide total span by two equal intervals.
Steps: Total span from zero to eight is 8.
There is one interior tick and hence TWO spaces.
WorkedExamples.Check: 0,4,8; do not call each gap one half of the unit from 0 to 1.

WorkedExamples.Title: Card B — quarters
WorkedExamples.Question: Card B goes from zero to one with three interior ticks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide one full unit into four equal intervals.
Steps: Three interior marks create four equal gaps.
First three interior points are 1/4, 2/4 and 3/4.

WorkedExamples.Title: Card F — sixths
WorkedExamples.Question: Card F goes from zero to one with five interior ticks.
WorkedExamples.Method: Divide the unit into six equal intervals.
Steps: Five interior marks give six equal spaces.

WorkedExamples.Title: Card H — thirds across two wholes
WorkedExamples.Question: Card H goes from 0 to 2 with two extra ticks within each unit.
WorkedExamples.Method: Three equal steps per complete whole.
Steps: One unit has two interior ticks => three equal intervals.
Across two wholes there are six intervals.
The first tick is 1/3; fourth tick is 4/3.

WorkedExamples.Title: Card I — halves across four wholes
WorkedExamples.Question: Card I shows labeled 0,2,4, with three ticks inside each interval from 0 to 2 and 2 to 4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Eight equal steps from zero to four.
Steps: Each two-unit span has four equal intervals.
A full 0-to-4 line has eight half-unit intervals.

WorkedExamples.Title: Andre and Clare — two interpretations
WorkedExamples.Question: Andre labels two half-length segments; Clare labels the middle point 1/2. Explain.
WorkedExamples.Method: Separate segment length from the point at a location.
Steps: 0 to halfway is a segment of length 1/2.
Halfway to 1 is another segment of length 1/2.
The halfway tick is at the number 1/2, so Andre describes lengths and Clare locates the number.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Both make sense in different ways
WorkedExamples.Check: A point label belongs at the tick; a length label can describe a gap.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat the count of tick marks as the number of equal intervals.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Two endpoints with three interior marks create four spaces, not three or five.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count gaps between ticks, including the two end gaps.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume card A 0-to-8's interval must be a fraction less than 1.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The two intervals cover eight units in total and each interval measures 4.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Say Andre or Clare must be wrong because their half labels are in different positions.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Andre describes half-LENGTHS, Clare locates 1/2 as a POINT.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Distinguish representation of a length from a number at a mark.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume every number line ends at 1.
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original cards A,C,D,E,G,H,I have endpoints beyond 1.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Preserve multi-whole scope; keep the 0-to-1 distance as the unit.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Write 1/3 after one fold that makes three visibly unequal gaps.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use congruent folds; teacher checks actual marks or drawings.

SummaryPoints: Number-line fractions use equal SPACES between ticks; numbers are at tick locations.
Original nine sorting cards: A 0–8 step4; B 0–1 quarters; C 0–3 halves; D 0–2 halves; E 0–4 ones; F 0–1 sixths; G 0–6 step2; H 0–2 thirds; I 0–4 halves.
The card sort is open: pupils classify cards with different valid rationales; teacher reviews groups and arguments.
Andre's two half labels measure segment lengths; Clare's half mark locates the numeric point.
Students physically fold separate lines into 2,3,4,6,8 equal intervals and locate first corresponding unit fractions.
Original 2021 publisher Cool-down, student PDF, tests and Stage D remain unverified; first-party diagrams only.
